South Africa Fixed Deposit Rates: 4.55% in Taiwan, 4.53% to Convert

2026.11.16 · Updated 2026.11.16 14 min read Scott Huang Banking

South Africa fixed deposit rates in November 2026 sit at two very different levels for the same currency. A one-year rand (ZAR) fixed deposit at E.SUN Bank in Taiwan is quoted at 4.55%, while the local South African money market reference range is 7.10–7.45%. Same currency, same money — the only variable is which country's account holds it.

That gap matters most to Taiwanese buyers preparing a Cape Town purchase. For most of them the rand is not a speculative position; it is the bridge money between selling a Taiwan asset and completing a Cape Town transfer, typically parked for a few months (two to four months is common; longer where non-resident documents are involved). To make the two sides comparable, every figure below uses a one-year annualised basis. On R1,000,000, the difference between 4.55% and 7.10% is R25,500 a year (about NT$51,255 at the site-wide 2.01 benchmark for November 2026) — and that gap is what this article measures. This article sets the published numbers side by side, then calculates how much of that gap currency movement can erase.

Key takeaway: E.SUN Bank quotes a one-year rand deposit at 4.55% (card dated 2026-11-10; the bank's rate page has been unreachable since 12 November), against a market-reference range of 7.10-7.45% for South African money market accounts (quote of 2026-10-02) - a gap of 2.55-2.90 percentage points. But the same currency costs 4.53% to move in and back out (Bank of Taiwan spot bid 1.895 / offer 1.985 on 2026-11-14), equal to 1.6-1.8 years of that South African spread. A one-year TWD time deposit pays 1.725% fixed (1.715% floating), and the CBC discount rate is 2.0%. ZAR/TWD fell 1.33% over 11-13 November 2026, about 46-52% of a year's spread. All figures are market-reference ranges, not promises of future returns.

Our position is stated up front: the rate gap usually exists, but currency moves can erase a large part of it within a very short time. Whether a rand deposit is a good idea depends entirely on whether the money is for a Cape Town payment in six months or parked capital for three years. Those two cases have opposite answers.

What Are South Africa Fixed Deposit Rates in November 2026?

South Africa fixed deposit rates in 2026 split into two tiers: E.SUN Bank in Taiwan pays 4.55%, local accounts pay 7.10–7.45%. The Taiwan rate card is dated 2026-11-10 and the South African quote 2026-10-02 — quotes from two different dates — early November in Taiwan versus early October in South Africa — not a same-day comparison.

The table below lists four published numbers with the date each was captured. When comparing South Africa fixed deposit interest rates, the date is the first thing to check: foreign currency rate cards change weekly, and quoting an October figure as "current" is the most common error in Chinese-language comparisons.

Why Are Taiwan Bank Rates Lower Than Local South African Rates?

Taiwan banks quote rand deposits as offshore retail products: 4.55% for one year in November 2026, below the 7.10–7.45% available in South Africa's local money market.

The first reason is funding cost. South African money market rates track the policy rate: the SARB repurchase rate has been 7.25% and the prime rate 10.75% since 2026-09-25. A Cape Town bank sourcing rand locally pays close to that level, so its short-dated deposit rates naturally sit around 7%.

The second reason is hedging and liquidity. A Taiwan bank taking rand deposits for a Cape Town purchase must price two risks: the currency risk of converting that rand back into TWD or USD later, and the liquidity risk of a thin ZAR market where raising rand at short notice is not easy. Both costs come straight out of the quoted rate. Rand is also a minor currency in Taiwan, so banks face no pressure to bid for deposits with high rates.

A useful mechanism analogy for a Cape Town property buyer: the same cup of coffee costs about 40% more inside an airport than on the street. The beans are identical — the price reflects where you are buying. A rand deposit works the same way: the rate reflects which market you stand in, not what the currency is worth. The analogy explains pricing tiers only; it does not rank one deposit route above another.

The 7.10–7.45% in South Africa is not automatically "better" either. It hands back exactly the costs the Taiwan bank removed: currency risk becomes yours, liquidity risk becomes yours, and the documentation and account upkeep become yours. For someone holding Cape Town property long term, those are costs they already carry. For someone simply chasing a little more interest from Taiwan, they are new costs.

(Source: SARB repo and prime rates read from resbank.co.za on 2026-11-06, effective 2026-09-25; E.SUN Bank ZAR rate card 2026-11-10; South African money market range 2026-10-02. Rates move with central bank policy and individual bank rate cards; they are not fixed income.)

The South African Reserve Bank's next Monetary Policy Committee decision is scheduled for 19 November 2026 (Thursday) at 15:00 SAST — 21:00 Taiwan time the same evening. The repo rate is 7.25% and prime 10.75%, effective 2026-09-25. What follows are three scenarios, not a forecast; this article takes no position on the outcome.

For anyone holding rand earmarked for a Cape Town transfer, the decisive column is timing, not rates. When the gap between the decision and your payment date is only a few days, waiting has almost no expected value while adding exposure to the decision-day currency move. If the money is genuinely idle for three years, the decision is one point on a rate path and does not justify reallocating.

One inference to avoid: a hike does not mean Cape Town prices must fall. Higher rates raise mortgage repayments and holding costs and squeeze local affordability, but prices also respond to supply, in-migration and currency. Does a 4.53% Round Trip Take 1.6-1.8 Years of Spread to Repay?

Bank of Taiwan quoted rand spot at 1.895 bid and 1.985 offer at 01:42 on 2026-11-14, so (1.985 - 1.895) / 1.985 = 4.53%. One round trip costs the equivalent of 1.6 to 1.8 years of the 2.55-2.90 point South African spread, and that cost is fixed the moment you walk into the bank - it has nothing to do with where the rand moves afterwards.

This is the section most readers skip and the one that decides the result. The 2.55-2.90 points above are an interest-rate gap; converting TWD into rand and back again adds a second cost, and that cost is not printed in the rate table. It sits between the bid and offer columns.

ItemValueCard timeNote
ZAR spot, bank buys1.8952026-11-14 01:42The price the bank pays when you convert back to TWD
ZAR spot, bank sells1.9852026-11-14 01:42The price you pay to buy rand
Bid-offer spread1.985 - 1.895 = 0.090sameTWD of spread per rand
Round-trip cost4.53%same0.090 / 1.985; value recovered 1.895 / 1.985 = 95.47%
TWD one-year time deposit (fixed)1.725%2026-11-14TWD benchmark; the floating column on the same card is 1.715%

Why use the offer of 1.985 as the denominator rather than the bid or the mid? Because the question is how much of the TWD I hand over disappears after one round trip. You pay 1.985 and receive 1.895, a recovery rate of 95.47%, a shortfall of 4.53%. Using the bid gives 4.75% and using the mid of 1.940 gives 4.64% - all three land near 4.5%, and this article uses the most direct cost-you-pay basis.

The card moves. The same Bank of Taiwan card showed 1.917 bid / 2.007 offer at 07:51 on 2026-11-13, the same 0.090 spread, which converts to 4.48%; this article uses the 2026-11-14 01:42 reading of 4.53%. The two readings differ by 0.05 points and change no conclusion, but the card follows the day's mid rate, and the rate that applies to you is the card at the moment you place the order.

One full trip makes it concrete. On R1,000,000 held for a year: entering at the 1.985 offer requires NT$1,985,000; one year at 4.55% earns R45,500, so principal plus interest is R1,045,500; converting back at the 1.895 bid returns NT$1,981,223. On an unchanged card, that is a loss of NT$3,777, or -0.19% in TWD. The same NT$1,985,000 in a one-year TWD time deposit (Bank of Taiwan, 1.725% carded on 2026-11-14) would earn NT$34,241, a difference of about NT$38,000. This calculation combines E.SUN Bank's 4.55% as carded on 2026-11-10 with Bank of Taiwan's spot card of 2026-11-14: it is an illustration built from two public Taiwan quotes, not a product offered by either bank, and it excludes currency movement, fees and taxes so that the conversion spread can be seen on its own.

Converted into time: the South African side earns 2.55-2.90 points more per year, so 4.53 / 2.90 = 1.56 years and 4.53 / 2.55 = 1.78 years. One round trip therefore takes 1.6 to 1.8 years of the spread just to break even (simple division, no compounding; compounding gives 1.55 and 1.76 years, the same conclusion), and the principal carries currency risk the whole time.

The cost is not a veto, and it has a specific dilution condition: hold longer than two years without further rand depreciation and the 4.53% is spread across the holding period, so its effect on the annual return shrinks (over three years, a simple straight-line split gives about 1.5% a year, ignoring time value). The question is not whether it is worth it, but how many years the money will stay.

Three boundaries have to travel with the 4.53%. First, it is a carded rate: larger tickets (in practice the equivalent of USD 50,000 and up) are usually negotiable at the counter, so the real spread is smaller; this article does not claim everyone pays 4.53%. Second, it is the spot rate: notes carry a visibly wider spread, but nobody funds a Cape Town purchase with cash notes, so notes are excluded. Third, 4.53% is a round trip: if the rand is eventually spent on a Cape Town purchase and never converted back, only the one-way cost applies, about 2.3% - precisely (1.985 - 1.940) / 1.985 = 2.27% against the 1.940 mid. Fees sit on top: a Taiwan outward transfer typically costs a few hundred TWD per transfer, correspondent and beneficiary bank charges are additional, and the South African receiving bank may charge its own inward fee, so the credited amount is what the advice shows. At a few hundred TWD per transfer that is about 0.03-0.05% of NT$1,985,000, but it is fixed, so the smaller the amount the larger the share. The tax treatment of the interest (South African withholding and Taiwan overseas income) is covered in the FAQ.

Currency moved in the same month. The ZAR/TWD mid rate went from 1.9971 on 11 November 2026 to 1.9706 on 13 November 2026, a cumulative 1.33% decline over three days. Against an annual spread of 2.55-2.90 points, those three days consumed 46-52% (1.33 / 2.90 = 45.9%; 1.33 / 2.55 = 52.2%). That is an event that already happened, not a projection; a three-day sample cannot be annualised, so no at-this-pace extrapolation appears here.

DateZAR/TWD midDaily changeSource

2026-11-121.9839-0.66%open.er-api.com (00:02 UTC)
2026-11-131.9706-0.67%open.er-api.com (00:02 UTC)
Three-day total--1.33%46-52% of a year's spread

The two costs have to be read separately because they behave differently. The 4.53% conversion spread is a one-off, predictable cost: it is on the card before you act, and a longer holding period dilutes it. The 1.33% currency decline is an ongoing, unpredictable move: it can only be measured after the fact, and it does not come back simply because you waited.

For anyone preparing a Cape Town purchase, first establish whether the money is ever converted back, because the two cases cost twice as much as each other. (1) The rand is spent directly on a Cape Town payment and never converted back: only the one-way cost applies, about 2.3%, which equals 0.78 to 0.89 years of spread (2.27 / 2.90 = 0.78; 2.27 / 2.55 = 0.89) - and three months of parking earns only 0.64 to 0.73 points, which does not repay it. (2) The money is converted back to TWD after a year: both legs total 4.53%, so 1.6 to 1.8 years of spread is needed. (3) The money stays in South Africa for three years, collecting rent: the conversion cost happens once, spreads to about 1.5% a year, and the spread has a chance to survive. All three cases share one conclusion: never trade a long-term rate advantage for short-term currency exposure.

What Documents Do Non-Residents Need to Open a South African Account?

South African banks run customer due diligence under FICA. The document list for a non-resident personal account that can hold a fixed deposit or money market balance is short, but the format requirements are strict. Rejections are almost always format problems, not eligibility problems — the same passport and the same address will fail if the paperwork is presented the wrong way.

1. Passport certification format

A plain "true copy" stamp is not accepted. A commissioner of oaths must confirm in English that the original was physically seen, add a true-likeness statement for the photo page, and include signature, date, address and occupation. If the Taiwanese notarisation is not issued in that format, the file is rejected in Cape Town and the round trip costs two to four weeks.

2. The TIN field

For a Taiwanese applicant the tax identification number is the national ID number. Many applicants leave it blank on the assumption that a non-resident has no South African tax number, but a blank field requires ticking Reason A, B or C with an explanation. An un-ticked blank is one of the most common rejection triggers.

3. The three-month rule on proof of address

Proof of address must be dated within three months of the application date. For a Cape Town account opening this deadline is what makes it dangerous: account opening itself takes four to eight weeks, so a document that is already two months old at submission can expire during the remediation stage and force the whole file to be rebuilt.

Once the account is open, the tax treatment of interest becomes the next question. Under section 50D(1)(a)(i)(bb) of the South African Income Tax Act and SARS Interpretation Note 115 (Issue 2, 30 June 2023), interest paid by a bank to a foreign person can qualify for exemption from the 15% interest withholding tax — but the boundaries in s50D(2) and (3), and the source definition in s50G, have to be read together. Taiwanese investors also still report foreign interest under Taiwan's alternative minimum tax regime. The two common Chinese-language claims — "completely tax free" and "always 15% withheld" — are both incomplete.

(Source: FICA document requirements and rejection patterns are compiled from DingYao and Crestline Advisory's actual submission experience; withholding tax provisions from section 50D(1)(a)(i)(bb) of the South African Income Tax Act and SARS Interpretation Note 115, Issue 2, 30 June 2023. Outcomes depend on the individual applicant and file; this is not tax advice.)

Can Fixed Deposit Interest Fund Retirement Cash Flow?

Yes, but only as one layer. Relying on South Africa rand deposit interest alone ties your retirement income to a moving interest rate and a moving exchange rate. Treating it as one of three layers is the version that actually holds up.

Start with the replacement ratio, and note that a South Africa rand deposit is the volatile layer here. On principal of NT$10,000,000 and annual living costs of NT$600,000 (NT$50,000 a month): a one-year rand deposit at 4.55% produces about NT$455,000 a year, a replacement ratio of roughly 76%; a TWD one-year time deposit at 1.725% produces about NT$172,500, or roughly 29%. Neither figure accounts for currency movement — if the rand weakens 5%, the TWD return on that 4.55% deposit is minus 0.45%.

LayerSourceCharacteristicMain risk
FirstSocial insurance annuities (labour insurance, national pension)Fixed amount, lifelong payout, most predictableBenefit levels and eligibility subject to policy change
SecondDeposit interest (TWD or rand fixed deposits)Controllable amount, adjustable through principalInterest rate changes, foreign currency movement
ThirdRental income (for example Cape Town property)Larger amounts, more correlated with living costsVacancy, management fees, maintenance, taxes, currency

Cape Town rent belongs in the third layer, not the second. Rent is operating income: management fees, maintenance reserves, vacant months and rental income tax all apply, none of which appear in a gross rental yield figure. When comparing Cape Town rent with rand deposit interest, use net amounts, otherwise both the property and your annual available cash will be overstated.

This article does not comment on the performance of any ETF or fund, does not argue that a higher distribution rate is better, and does not rank Cape Town property above rand deposits. For retirement cash flow, what decides the outcome is the proportion across the three layers and whether the volatility of each layer can be absorbed by living costs — not the headline return of any single product.

(Source: rates from E.SUN Bank 2026-11-10 and Bank of Taiwan 2026-11-14 rate cards; replacement ratios calculated here from the stated principal and living cost assumptions, not published by any institution. The calculation excludes taxes, fees and currency movement; actual results vary with rates, exchange rates and personal circumstances, and are not guaranteed.)

Taiwan or South Africa: What Decides Which Account Fits?

Rand deposits in 2026 are best judged by deadline: money needed within 12 months sits in Taiwan, longer-idle amounts above R1,000,000 favour South Africa.

This is a cost comparison for information only (not investment advice): it compares what each route charges, not what it promises.

A: Cape Town payment within 12 monthsTransfer, deposit, taxes and feesTaiwan rand account (demand or sub-one-year term)The four to eight week account opening cycle removes payment flexibility, and currency moves hit the purchase price directly
B: Idle 1–3 years, above R1,000,000Long-term parking while waiting for entry timingSouth African local money market account (reference 7.10–7.45%)Beyond 12 months the spread exceeds the fixed cost of opening and documenting an account
C: Already hold Cape Town property, collecting rentReinvesting rent, reserving for taxesSouth African local account, same market as the incomeRent and taxes are already in South Africa; the money avoids repeated conversion

What the three scenarios share is that the deciding variables are deadline and purpose, not the interest rate. The same 4.55% and 7.10% mean "not worth opening a Cape Town account for 2.5 points" in scenario A, and "R25,500 a year, R76,500 over three years, worth doing" in scenario B. That judgement requires no currency forecast.

Published bank cards differ in structure: south africa term deposit rates at the large banks, including FNB south africa fixed deposit rates, are republished monthly on each bank's own site, and the tier depends on amount and term. This article compares the local money market reference range rather than reproducing any single bank card, because those cards change every month and would be stale by publication.

Second, every TWD figure above uses the site benchmark of 2.01 for November 2026 (month range 1.98–2.01), and currency movement changes the answer. Work out your own number before deciding where the money sits — that beats any comparison article, including this one.

FAQ

Are rand fixed deposits worth it?

You may be thinking: "4.55% is more than double the TWD rate, so converting and locking in is the obvious move." What is missed, for a Cape Town transfer funded from Taiwan, is treating the interest rate as the return. The 4.55% is paid in rand; converting back to TWD applies the exchange rate a second time, and depreciation comes straight out of the result. The November 2026 figures for a Cape Town transfer are a 4.55% one-year rand deposit at E.SUN Bank (card dated 2026-11-10) against a 1.725% one-year TWD time deposit at Bank of Taiwan - but the same currency costs 4.53% to move in and back out, which equals 1.6-1.8 years of the South African spread. The E.SUN rate is the 2026-11-10 reading (its rate page has been unreachable since 2026-11-12) and the Bank of Taiwan card is listed 2026-11-14, and the FX quotes come from open.er-api.com on 2026-11-11 (1.9971) and 2026-11-12 (1.9839).

Is the 4.55% one-year rand rate at E.SUN Bank fixed?

You may be thinking: "The card says 4.55%, so once I deposit, 4.55% is locked for the whole term." The error is confusing a single day's South Africa rate card quote with a contract term. Foreign currency deposits come in fixed-rate and floating-rate versions, and only the fixed-rate column locks the rate for the term. The 4.55% cited here is the fixed-rate column for a one-year ZAR time deposit at E.SUN Bank on 2026-11-10; the rate that applies to you is the card on the day you place the order. On the same card, six and nine months also show 4.55%, while one and three months show 4.50%. The E.SUN foreign currency deposit rate card (2026-11-10 reading) lists rand demand at 1.8%, one month 4.50%, three months 4.50%, six months 4.55%, nine months 4.55% and one year 4.55%.

Is opening a South African account for 7% safe?

You may be thinking: "7% is two and a half points more, opening an account sounds simple, so there is not much risk." The problem in a Cape Town account opening is not whether the bank is sound; it is conflating three different risks: bank credit risk, currency risk, and documentation and process risk. The 7.10–7.45% is a market reference range, not a capital guarantee. Local South African money market rates used by Cape Town banks track the SARB repo rate of 7.25% (effective 2026-09-25). The higher return exists because you carry currency and liquidity risk, plus four to eight weeks of account opening time and the spread on repatriation. SARB repo and prime were read from resbank.co.za on 2026-11-06; the local money market range comes from the site's 2026-10-02 quote; opening timelines come from DingYao and Crestline Advisory submission records.

Is 15% tax withheld on South African deposit interest?

You may be thinking: "Foreigners always lose 15%, so there is little left after withholding." What is missed is the eligibility test: South Africa provides an exemption for interest paid to a foreign person, and the outcome depends on whether the account and the funds meet the section 50D conditions, not on nationality. Under section 50D(1)(a)(i)(bb) of the Income Tax Act and SARS Interpretation Note 115 (Issue 2, 30 June 2023), interest paid by a bank to a foreign person can be exempt from the 15% withholding tax, but the conditions in s50D(2) and (3) and the source test in s50G still apply. The provisions are published on the SARS website as Interpretation Note 115, Issue 2, 30 June 2023; separately, Taiwan still requires foreign interest to be included in the alternative minimum tax base, so the two jurisdictions are handled apart.

Will the 19 November 2026 SARB decision change a deposit I already placed?

You may be thinking: "Once the decision lands my deposit rate will change too, so I should wait for the result first." The error is treating the South Africa rate on new placements and the rate on an existing fixed deposit as the same thing. A fixed-rate deposit does not reprice during its term; what changes is the rate on rollovers and new placements. The SARB decision is scheduled for 19 November 2026 (Thursday) at 15:00 SAST, with repo at 7.25% and prime at 10.75% since 2026-09-25. The three scenarios — hold, plus 25bp, minus 25bp — affect new rates and the currency, not a fixed rate already contracted. The decision date was captured from zaim.com on 2026-11-13 and matches the SARB official calendar; repo and prime come from resbank.co.za read on 2026-11-06.

The three most common failure points
